A public utility for street art.

A phone already reads menus and mail out loud. Gestalt points it at the city's walls: stand in front of any mural and hear what's painted there, who made it, and why, in more than one language.

A passion project by Philadelphia designer Chris Carter · DesignPhiladelphia Awards 2026 nominee

Access is not generosity. It is the removal of a barrier that should not have existed.

A wall you understand is a wall you belong to.

A mural isn't decoration. It's an argument, a memory, a joke, a grief, made public on purpose. Taking one in should reach everyone on the sidewalk, not just the people who can read it at a glance.

For years, software has been able to say what sits in front of you. The tools that read the practical world can name a menu, a dollar bill, even a painted wall, and there they stop. Gestalt was built for what comes after: a description written the way people actually write about art, tied to the exact wall you're standing at, reviewed by a human describer before it ever plays.

What a visitor hears.

Persistence, a mural by Jason Andrew Turner: a towering blue wall, a figure in a red dress scattered with white dots. A generic caption would stop at blue wall. Press play and hear what a describer wrote for the person standing in front of it. No front desk, no borrowed device.

That's the whole idea in one wall: what you just did with your thumb, a neighbor does with their phone, at any mural in the city.

Four neighbors. One wall.

01

Blind and low vision Philadelphians

The city's public art on your own terms, described the moment you stand in front of it. No help required, no one to ask.

02

Neighbors who don't read English

A mural explained in a language you actually read, so the city's walls speak to all of it, not part.

03

The city and its institutions

A live, honest picture of what's described and what isn't. The ADA accountability a public collection owes, ready the morning of the meeting.

04

Artists and Mural Arts partners

Every description carries the artist's name and points people back to the work. The wall stays the artist's; Gestalt makes sure more of the city arrives at it.
